newsitem.title: UK: Copper ends with pared gains, LME seeks direction.
newsitem.headline: Copper ends with pared gains, LME seeks direction.

text.p: Copper prices stepped back from their highs during Wednesday afternoon LME trading, but still closed steadier as did most of the metals complex.
However, the pace of trade in all markets was slow, with the next major move difficult to discern now that the investment funds have stepped aside for the moment.
"It has been a fairly slow day throughout -- there's not much in the way of trade business or spec business," one floor trader said.

If anything the investment funds may have moved towards a short stance in the market, given that the summer period is nearing when metal offtake slows. Also, monetary policy trends in the U.S. suggest a tightening may take place, which would cool the economy, some said.

Others were unsure, however. "Who can say in early April what the third quarter is going to be like? It just needs the Chinese to buy (copper) in a big way to get all the markets motoring. Then you'll get funds buying and covering," another said.

Copper prices performed adequately throughout after recapturing $2,300 with stocks falling 5,350 tonnes due to drawdowns in Singapore and Hamburg. But the market stalled just above $2,310 and settled back on the kerb to close at $2,307, a net gain of $15 from Tuesday.
The cash/threes backwardation edged out to around $48/51 by the close, although spread operations were not significant.
Aluminium flipped up to a high-point of $1,597 during the kerb, when buy-stops were triggered above the $1,590 level -- an area where 100-day moving average resistance was pegged.

But there was little followthrough and not enough impetus to carry the market above $1,600, and although the market was higher and stocks fell by 2,275 tonnes, prices may fall back again. Last trade was at $1,592, up $9.50 from Tuesday.

Nickel prices reached a high water-mark of $7,500 in mid-afternoon trading before backtracking from this important chart objective. Despite some stern selling at this level the market nevertheless maintained a strong technical bounce from Monday's lows.
Traders said the market is in limbo on the charts, but could well subside back to levels nearer $7,100. Last trade was at $7,490, up $185 from the previous kerb.

Zinc business was fairly routine thoughout the session, with a generally steadier trend a reflection of a 2,075-tonne stock decline. Prices movements were thin, however, and last trade was at $1,266, up $6.
The lead market saw little interest and as a consequence hardly budged during the day. There was a modest dip towards $650, but last business at $652 was just $1 down from Tuesday.
Tin business was equally uninspiring, with the market gradually edging up from overnight levels to end at $5,760, a $20 advance. The alloy market was marked up fractionally to $1,475/1,480 a tonne.
